strengths: Learning Sinkhorn initializations from adversarially generated distribution pairs is a useful, well-motivated combination. Training without examples from the eventual application dataset offers a potentially valuable distinction from dataset-specific learned initializers.

The reported improvements over all-ones initialization are consistent across four test sets. Tables 1–2 support average iteration reductions of approximately 16% and 33% at marginal-error tolerances of 1e-3 and 1e-2, respectively. Evaluating marginal feasibility alongside transport-cost error and runtime strengthens this evidence.

The manuscript explains the connection between dual potentials and Sinkhorn scaling vectors clearly. Architecture specifications, training pseudocode, hyperparameters, and a code link make the basic approach understandable.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not establish the benefit of the principal methodological contribution. There is no comparison against training on fixed random samples or using an untrained generator, so the value of adversarial sample generation remains unknown. Initialization experiments compare only against all-ones initialization, omitting the relevant initializers discussed in the related work. Figure 3 compares loss functions using potential MSE, rather than subsequent Sinkhorn convergence or matched training cost; it therefore does not establish superiority over the cited learned approach. These missing comparisons substantially weaken the contribution relative to prior work.

The claim of generalization to any pair of distributions of fixed dimension exceeds the evidence. All experiments use 28-by-28 images, the same squared-Euclidean cost, positive smoothing, and a single regularization value. Transfer to several datasets is encouraging, but does not establish universal performance even within this fixed geometry. Testing concentrated or strongly imbalanced distributions and varying epsilon would directly probe the stated generality and the motivation for learning epsilon-independent potentials.

Section 3.3 draws a stronger conclusion from Proposition 7 than the proposition supports. The result bounds entropic dual objective suboptimality, not the distance between regularized and unregularized potentials or the resulting Sinkhorn iteration count. Unregularized optimal potentials can remain nonunique after fixing their additive constant, and exponentiation can magnify potential errors at small epsilon. Moreover, the stated bound mn*epsilon is approximately 153.7 in the experimental setting, making it quantitatively uninformative relative to the cost scale. The proof supports an objective-value statement, but does not establish the claimed approximation of potentials.

The standalone barycenter application is insufficiently validated. Figure 7 provides recognizable images but no comparison with reference barycenters, objective values, or computational costs. The error-cancellation argument assumes zero-mean prediction errors without evidence; even unbiased objective estimates at fixed inputs would not establish accurate minimizers when optimizing over those inputs. Consequently, this experiment does not convincingly support using the approximator independently.

Secondary reporting gaps limit reproducibility and assessment of practical gains. The manuscript does not specify test-pair counts, independent training runs, how confidence intervals were constructed, or the test-time smoothing constant. Numerical precision and stabilization are also consequential at epsilon = 0.00025, where directly forming the stated Gibbs kernel can underflow; clipping the initialization does not resolve kernel underflow. Explicit inference and C-transform timing, together with the number of solves needed to amortize the reported three-hour training cost, would clarify the practical significance.
